d.t: Used in embarrassment.
d.e: I fear that I was rude to her.

d.t: Used when worried or concerned.
d.e: I fear that her business will fail.

d.t: Used for dramatic effect or emphasis.
d.e: She ate, I fear.

d.t: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see I, fear.
d.e: I fear spiders.

d.t: An agreement or understanding in sentiment or belief.
Synonym of I kid you not (Used to insist that one is telling the truth)
d.e: ‘My God, Steve – are you fucking with me?’ ‘I fuck you not, my friend. You guys are gonna be on Friends.’

d.t: Supposing that, assuming that, in the circumstances that; suppositive used to introduce a condition that may be (or prove to be) either true or false.
d.e: I'll do it next week if I have time.

d.t: Supposing that; used with past or past perfect subjunctive to indicate a counterfactual or hypothetical condition.
d.e: If she hadn't told me, I wouldn't know.

d.t: Considering the fact that; given that; introducing a condition that is known to be true.
d.e: The drain's blocked — and if the drain's blocked, the water won't flow.

d.t: When; whenever; every time that.
d.e: If you heat water to 100° C, it boils.

d.t: Although; used to introduce a concession; may..but.
d.e: He was a great friend, if a little stingy at the bar.

d.t: While; used to introduce a contrast.
d.e: If tea is expensive, coffee is completely unaffordable.

d.t: Whether; used to introduce a noun clause, an indirect question, that functions as the direct object of certain verbs.
d.e: I don't know if I want to go or not.

d.t: Introducing a relevance conditional; in case.
d.e: I have leftover cake if you want some.

d.t: An uncertainty, possibility, condition, doubt etc.
d.e: The board can't approve this project; there are too many ifs.

d.t: Is equivalent to; implies and is implied by; is true and false in the same cases as.
d.e: A rectangle is a square if and only if all four of its sides have the same length.

d.t: Synonym of if (with added intensity)
d.e: I'll let you go to the concert if and only if you clean your room.

d.t: At the time of an event, contingent on that event happening at all.
d.e: Near-synonym: as and when

d.t: Used to suggest or state tentatively that something may be the case (often the opposite of something previously implied).
d.e: The situation is, if anything, worsening rather than improving.

d.t: Used in questions when the speaker does not know for sure if the listener will have an answer.
d.e: What can you tell me, if anything, about this book?

d.t: Synonym of if anything.
If at any time; if at all.
d.e: I seldom if ever travel abroad.

d.t: Used to emphasize the truth of a characterization.
d.e: He's a plagiarist if ever there was one.

w: if i do say so myself

d.t: Appended to praise of oneself or one's own doings, as a form of modesty.
d.e: A rather dashing outfit, even if I do say so.

d.t: Synonym of if ever there was one.
d.e: There's a messed-up face if I ever saw one.

d.t: Without any following verb, implies a request to interrupt, to speak at length, or to take control, often when the speaker can introduce new, unexpected information or, alternatively, when the speaker disapproves of how a task was done and proposes to redo it.
Used to soften the effect of a statement that is self-aggrandizing or is embarrassing to the listener.
A phrase said to introduce advice, i.e. to express what one would do in the interlocutor's situation.
Synonym of if so be.
If a certain condition were not met; used to indicate that a particular person, event, etc. prevented a certain outcome.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see if, it, you, please.
d.e: The Emperour ſaid foꝛ his ſaik that you bought, / Withouttin feir ſhew me your minde and thought / Ye ſhall me finde to you truſt and conſtant, / Vnto your health there is nocht ye ſhall want, / Therefoꝛe ſhew fooꝛth your minde if it you pleaſe, / What ye ſhall ſay nothing ſhall…

d.t: Used to characterize a look of strong hostility.
A type of money collected from earnings on one race which is then automatically applied to a subsequent race in the case when an if-bet is placed.
If necessary; if there is a need.
d.e: And I am quite sure that Max Carrados won't walk in here without making it certain that if he doesn't soon come out again the C.I.D. will smash down the door if need be to find out what has happened.

d.t: If need be; if there is a need.
d.e: April 20, 1964, Nelson Mandela, speech at trial I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination. I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities. It is an…

d.t: Indicates that a statement is true in the event that a condition is not satisfied.
d.e: The plant will die if not watered.

d.t: Indicates that one statement at least is true, and possibly a second, stronger statement is true; perhaps even.
d.e: He did as well as expected, if not better.

d.t: Indicates that one statement is true, but a second is not; but not.
d.e: I saw that he had improved his manners if not his scruffy appearance.

d.t: If (something) were not (or had not been) there; in the absence of (something); without.
d.e: If not for her surgical skill, you'd be dead now, so some appreciation may be in order.

d.t: At the very least; as a minimum.
d.e: Briefly, they had threatened to turn the game upside-down after Wayne Rooney’s first-ever World Cup goal made it 1-1 after 75 minutes. If nothing else, England had shown perseverance but, then again England always show qualities of endurance.

d.t: If not older; at least.
d.e: He must be fifty if he's a day.

d.t: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see if, only.
d.e: It made me feel better, if only for a moment.

d.t: I wish that; would (that) (archaic). Signifies a wish or desire for the present or the future.
d.e: If only I could win the lottery.

d.t: I wish that; would (that) (archaic). Signifies a regret about an action in the past.
d.e: If only I had listened to my parents.

d.t: Even if for no other reason than; only just.
d.e: I was pretty sure what I wanted, but I still tried on another if only to make sure.

d.t: Signifies a hypothetical or wishful precondition, or one which would be simple but is nonetheless unlikely, for a hypothetical, counterfactual, or future outcome.
d.e: He could be a great student if only he got [or: if he only got] a little non-judgmental encouragement.

d.t: Contingent upon the possibility or convenience of the request.
If such is the case.
d.e: Are you free? If so, let's go out for a meal tonight. If not, then it'll be Sat.

d.t: If; if it happens (that); supposing that.
or even less, at most
d.e: My car is so old that, if I were to sell it, I would get a hundred pounds, if that.

d.t: Used to introduce one's opinion, without being asked for it.
d.e: B.W. Wooster: If you ask me, art is responsible for most of the trouble in the world. R. Jeeves: An interesting theory, sir. Would you care to expatiate upon it? B.W. Wooster: As a matter of fact, no, Jeeves. The thought just occurred to me, as thoughts do. R. Jeeves: Very good…

w: if you know what i mean

d.t: Used to allude to something unsaid or hinted at.
d.e: He seemed a little too interested in the details, if you know what I mean [implying that perhaps he had ulterior motives].

d.t: Used as a rhetorical question to confirm attention, understanding, or agreement at the end of an utterance or each segment thereof; synonym of do you know what I'm saying.
d.e: Then you've got to jiggle it just right, if you know what I mean, before you can get it to come out of there.

d.t: Please, kindly; used in giving a non-concrete instruction.
d.e: But imagine, if you like, a world where climate change did not exist.

d.t: So to speak, like; used to indicate that a description is not standard.
d.e: This band's genre can be described as, if you like, New Wave or Post-Punk.

d.t: Please.
d.e: 1906, Edith Nesbit, The Railway Children, Chapter 4: The engine-burglar, The engine-driver and fireman did not see her. They were leaning out on the other side, telling the Porter a tale about a dog and a leg of mutton. "If you please," said Roberta--but the engine was blowing…

d.t: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see if, you, please.
d.e: Say you ſo, Sir, why then you are oblig’d to me for telling your fortune beforehand; you may avoid it if you pleaſe; I have giv’n you warning.

d.t: Used to convey lack of agreement together with a refusal to enter into or continue an argument.
Please, kindly; used in giving a non-concrete instruction.
d.e: But imagine, if you will, a world where these logistical problems were solved.

d.t: So to speak, like; used to indicate that a description is not standard.
d.e: These are "partial artifacts", if you will: the imaging process has merely amplified flaws that were already present in the original.

d.t: Used in conceding a description or choice of terms.
d.e: He wasn't a very honest person; a liar, if you will.

d.t: Synonym of material conditional.
A complex system of divination in Yoruba religion.
A construct in source code that allows another part of the code to run only if a specified identifier is defined in the program.
Of dubious authenticity, legitimacy or legality.
d.e: He's selling new CD players for £20 each – that sounds a bit iffy to me.

d.t: Uncertain or chancy; risky.
d.e: The weather is still iffy for Saturday's rocket launch.

d.t: A particular drug used in chemotherapy.
A section of a web page that can act as the container for a second separate page or resource.
d.e: This enabled developers to forego framesets altogether and simply place invisible iframes (through the use of CSS) on a page to enable client-server communication.

d.t: A kind of djinn mentioned in the Qur'an.
A demon, evil spirit, often associated with the underworld.
d.e: Then she flew firmament-wards to circle it, as was her custom, and met an Ifrit on the wing who saluted her and she said to him, "Whence comest thou?"

d.t: A species of passerine bird endemic to New Guinea, in full the blue-capped ifrit.
The evening meal that breaks each day's fast during Ramadan, traditionally beginning with dates and water.
d.e: Iftars can be social events, where people congregate to eat and socialize.
